requirement.title: the student is trained and measured on commerce
requirement.text:
Run `distill.ipynb` on a Colab T4 with the bundle from `bundle.py`:
- Qwen2.5-Coder-3B queries, with the teacher round-trip filter (`--llm-top 10`).
- Three students: ettin-17m, ettin-32m, and ettin-32m with LoRA 16.

Report commerce MRR, val doc MRR and val LLM MRR against MiniLM 0.649, gte-small+WQL 0.700 and
jina+WQL 0.775.

Before the 20k-query run, check a sample of 50 of the 3B model's queries by eye. The 1.5B
generator's first queries mostly restated the symbol's name.

requirement.title: speed is re-timed in fp32
requirement.text:
The speed gate measured int8, but students must ship fp32 (dynamic int8 took ettin-17m from 0.40
to 0.02 MRR).
- Re-time MiniLM, ettin-17m and ettin-32m in fp32 on the same 3,698 cards.
- Re-check granite-small-r2's zero-shot score, which was also int8.
- Add `--fp32` to `speed_gate.py`.

requirement.title: a student ships only if it clears the gate
enough questions to tell conditions apart
the lab compares encoders as well as conditions
requirement.text:
`prepare.py --model` and `--wql` already re-index the repos. Run the grid for:
- MiniLM, with and without WQL-path cards;
- the distilled student, once it exists.

That makes the lab the downstream check for Track A, not just commerce MRR.

requirement.title: retrieval is measured without a model
requirement.text:
`ctx_facts` (the share of facts present in the context) needs no LLM, and it is what most
retrieval changes should move.
- Add a `--retrieval-only` mode to `run.py`, so a ranking change can be checked in seconds before
  spending GPU time.
- Keep LLM runs for changes to how context is packed.

requirement.title: documentation results carry their line span
requirement.text:
Section cards record only `attrs.section` (`dense/src/transformers/docs.ts`). Give every doc card
the section's `startLine` and `endLine`, and give each part its own lines within them. A search
hit on part 10 then says where the section starts, and a client can read it all without
re-parsing headings the way the lab does.

requirement.title: search can return source, not only cards
Go package-level variables are symbols
requirement.text:
`structural/src/mappings/go.json` maps `const_spec` but has no `var_spec`, so no Go `var` is a
symbol. gin's `default404Body` (in a `var ( … )` block in gin.go) has no card and cannot be found.
- Map `var_spec` to `variable`, with its identifier as the name, inside blocks as well.
- Check the other mappings for the same gap with module-level values: Python, Rust `static`, and
  Java fields.

requirement.title: the existing propagation experiment is measured
D1 and D2 are tried in the lab first
requirement.text:
Add an `anvesa-graph` lab condition with sibling parts (D1) and one-hop packing (D2), using
`anvesa callers`, `callees` and `neighbors` at first, so nothing in anvesa changes until it shows
a gain. It must:
- beat `anvesa-code` on facts in context at the same budget;
- reach `gin-not-found`;
- not lose on any question `anvesa-code` already answers.

If it does, move it into `search --source` (#req-search-source).

requirement.title: D3 and D4 are measured on commerce and the lab
requirement.text:
Ranking changes are measured on both commerce MRR (43 queries) and the lab's facts in context.
Implement test → subject (D3) and the graph lane (D4) behind an `experimental` flag, the way
`cardPath` is. Keep one only if it improves both without slowing search by more than 150 ms.

requirement.title: D6 waits for evidence
a tree ranker reorders the top results, behind a flag
requirement.text:
Port ltr.py's features and an exported XGBoost model to the retriever, behind an `experimental`
flag the way `cardPath` is:
- The features are computed in TypeScript from what search already has: first-stage scores,
  BM25 on card and intent text, name, path and kind, same-file count and call degree.
- The trees are evaluated in plain TypeScript from the exported JSON, with no ONNX runtime.
- It ships only if it improves gen-lab MRR and commerce MRR, and adds no more than 5 ms.
- `--explain` names the features that moved a hit.

requirement.title: anvesa records what happened to its results, in medha
requirement.text:
After a search, record a medha episode for each shown hit an agent acted on:
- **applied:** the agent opened or edited it;
- **skipped:** a hit ranked above an applied one that it passed over;
- nothing for hits below the last one used, which are unknown rather than negative.

The episode carries the query, the ranker version, each hit's rank and its feature vector, so a
ranker can be retrained without re-running search. Episodes stay in the local medha log; they leave
the machine only through medha's own sync, which is opt-in.

requirement.title: the ranker retrains from usage
requirement.text:
`anvesa rank train` fits a new ranker from medha episodes, with the bench queries as a floor:
- Use only queries with at least one applied hit.
- Weight each label by medha's Wilson lower bound, so a pattern seen twice counts for less than one
  seen two hundred times.
- Report the new ranker on the bench before it is used, next to the current one.

requirement.title: medha decides which ranker is trusted
requirement.text:
Each trained ranker is a medha entity:
- It starts on **probation** and is used on a share of searches.
- Its guard: bench MRR no lower than the current ranker's, and an applied rate in live use at
  least as high, by Wilson lower bound.
- It becomes **trusted** (the default) only after the guard passes.
- If it starts losing, it is **quarantined** and search falls back to the previous trusted ranker,
  or to the first stage.

`medha show` explains why a ranker is where it is.

requirement.title: anvesa records what happened to its results, in medha
requirement.text:
After a search, record a medha episode for each shown hit an agent acted on:
- **applied:** the agent opened or edited it;
- **skipped:** a hit ranked above an applied one that it passed over;
- nothing for hits below the last one used, which are unknown rather than negative.

A hit whose edit then passes a medha guard (tests, lint) is the strongest label, and is recorded
as such.

The episode carries the query, the ranker version, each hit's rank and its feature vector, so a
ranker can be retrained without re-running search. It also records whether the search was an
exploration search (#req-ltr-adaptive) and which hits were swapped. Episodes stay in the local
medha log; they leave the machine only through medha's own sync, which is opt-in.

requirement.title: the ranker adapts per repo without learning its own bias
requirement.text:
- **Warm start.** Once enough new episodes exist (a starting bar: 50 queries with an applied hit),
  continue training from the trusted ranker with a few shallow trees, rather than refitting from
  scratch. Each result is a new version on probation (#req-ltr-governed).
- **Global plus per-repo.** The shipped global ranker is shared. Each repo gets its own small stack
  of correction trees on top, and scores are global plus correction. A repo with little evidence
  keeps an empty or tiny stack.
- **Position bias.** Agents open top results more because they are on top. Weight each label by
  the inverse of how often its rank is opened regardless of relevance, so the ranker does not
  reinforce its own order.
- **Exploration.** On a small share of searches (a starting bar: 5%), swap two adjacent hits in the
  top 5. These searches estimate position bias, and let a probation version be compared with the
  trusted one by interleaving their results.
- **Guarded.** A per-repo stack is promoted only if it does not lose on that repo's past episodes
  or on the bench.

requirement.title: anvesa generates intent cards at index time
requirement.text:
- A bundled code LLM writes a few example queries per symbol. They are stored as an `intent`
  channel and fused with the card at weight 0.5, with the hub penalty at 0.3 and the path line
  dropped (the gen-lab setup).
- Generation is incremental: only symbols whose card text changed are regenerated, keyed by a hash
  of the card.
- It runs in the background after the normal index. Search works without intent cards and uses
  them as they arrive.
- Queries that name their own symbol are dropped before embedding.
- It can be turned off, and the model is downloaded on first use, not bundled into the package.

requirement.title: the generator is chosen on laptop CPU cost and bench MRR
requirement.text:
Before shipping, measure each candidate quantized for CPU (GGUF q4 via llama.cpp, or int8 ONNX):
- seconds per 1,000 symbols on a Windows laptop and a Mac, CPU only;
- bench MRR with the quantized model's queries, against 0.566 (1.5B in fp16) and 0.543 (card only);
- disk and memory.

The candidates are qwen2.5-coder-1.5B and -3B, and the best student from the distillation work. Pick
the smallest that stays within noise of the 1.5B. If none fits a reasonable first-index budget,
keep generation opt-in.

requirement.title: the oracle headroom is measured before anything is built
requirement.text:
The simulated numbers above become a lab script, `qopt.py` in the gen-lab, that reproduces them
from stored vectors. Then a sample of ~60 queries (all 24 first-stage misses at 10, plus ~36
hits, spread over the 8 repos) gets a hand-written oracle WQL, stored next to each query as
`wql = "…"` in `bench/<repo>.toml`. That WQL is the best one a developer who knows the repo's
layout would write, without looking at the gold. Each is run through `anvesa query` on the lab
clone and combined with the first stage in each mode (hard, pre-filter, soft, top-30, fused).

Done when:
- the report gives MRR / R@10 / R@30 per mode, with paired CIs against the first stage, on both
  first stages;
- it gives the into/out-of-top-10 counts;
- it lists the oracle WQLs that matched nothing or excluded the gold, by language.

H1 holds if the hand-written oracle gains ≥ +0.02 R@10 on the sample in some mode. If it does not,
stop here and record why.

requirement.title: the break-even curve is part of every predictor's report
requirement.text:
`qopt.py` reports, for kind, directory and identifier constraints, the noisy-oracle curve (MRR
and R@10 vs error rate *p*), per combination mode. Each predictor's report then gives three
numbers: how often it fires, how accurate it is where it fires, and where that accuracy lands on
the curve.

A predictor proceeds only if its measured accuracy is above break-even for the mode it would use.

requirement.title: a query set phrased the way developers type
conjunctions never lose what the literal query found
requirement.text:
The retriever gains the combination modes above for *derived* conjunctions:
- soft boost, top-k reorder, and fused rewrites, alongside today's hard filter;
- hard mode pre-filters inside the dense scan rather than filtering a fetched 500.

The fallback rules hold:
- an empty, unparseable or near-universal WQL runs the query as typed;
- the literal query is always one of the fused inputs.

User-written conjunctions keep today's hard semantics.

Done when, on the bench, no optimizer variant moves a gold hit out of the top 30 on more than 1%
of queries (H3), and a test covers each fallback.

requirement.title: rule-based extraction, grounded in the index
the rewrite is visible and can be turned off
requirement.text:
Search output says what was searched when it differs from what was typed (`searched as: save user
&& //class[@name="UserRepo"]//method`). JSON output carries the rewrite and each part's source.
`--literal` (and a config key) turns the optimizer off.

requirement.title: predicted constraints reach the ranker as features
a small tagger for latent kind and area, only if the rules leave headroom
requirement.text:
B3: predicts kind (~10 classes) and area (the repo's top directories, or "none") from the query.
It abstains below a confidence threshold. Trained on Colab from the intent cards' (intent text →
card kind, path) pairs plus the dev query set's training split. There are two inputs to compare:
- the dense query embedding, cheap but maybe redundant with the ranking;
- a text-only head, character n-grams.

Proceeds only if #req-qopt-oracle shows headroom on queries the rules do not fire on. Done when
its accuracy where it fires clears #req-qopt-break-even for top-30 reorder, and the leave-one-repo-out
ΔMRR on the bench is ≥ 0.

requirement.title: an LLM rewriter, constrained and validated, as an opt-in
requirement.text:
B4: a 0.5–1.5B model on Colab first. It gets the query and a compact repo outline (top
directories, top classes) and writes 1–3 WQL candidates under a grammar constraint (a GBNF / regex
grammar derived from `structural/src/wql.ts`). Each candidate is validated by running it, and
discarded if it is empty or near-universal. The survivors are fused with the literal query.

Measured on both query sets against B1 + B2, with CPU latency timed on the laptop in fp32 and q4.
It may only be an opt-in `--rewrite` or an `anvesa ask` / agent step unless its p95 is under the
interactive budget.

requirement.title: relation queries go to the graph
requirement.text:
"who calls X", "what uses Y", "implementations of Z", "tests for X" resolve X against the symbol
table. Then they answer from `callers` / `callees` / `dependents` / SCIP `references:type`, with
the relation's targets seeded into search (plan/connection-aware-retrieval, track D). If X does
not resolve, the query runs as NL.

Measured on the dev set's `relation` and `test` styles. The gin unmatched-routes case (`NoRoute`
vs `TestNoRoute`, `callers serveError`) is a named test.

requirement.title: per-language limits on what the optimizer emits
requirement.text:
A table, in code, of which constraint kinds the optimizer may emit per language, derived from the
mappings' real coverage. Initially:
- no `[@name]` on C/C++ functions;
- no property kind for C#;
- no constant/variable kind for Go var blocks until #req-go-var-blocks.

The oracle run (#req-qopt-oracle) lists the WQL that failed by language. That list is the
evidence for each row.

requirement.title: the optimizer ships on by default only through a gate
a small network says, with a probability, whether a query is pure or decomposable
requirement.text:
B3, the preferred builder: a tiny network that runs in-process and is fast and private (ONNX,
well under 1 ms on a laptop CPU, a few MB at most, no LLM, no network). It emits calibrated
probabilities, not labels:

- **Gate.** p(decomposable). Below the threshold the query runs exactly as typed. On the 241 NL
  bench queries it should be low for ≥ 95% of them.
- **Heads**, read only when the gate fires:
  - p(kind = k) over ~10 outline kinds;
  - per-token p(identifier) spans, kept only if the span resolves in the index;
  - p(relation ∈ {calls, called-by, uses, implements, tests});
  - area, scored per candidate directory as p(dir | query, dir name) rather than over a fixed
    label set, since directories differ per repo.

How the probabilities are used:
- Each emitted constraint carries its probability into the combination mode. It is applied
  hard only above the break-even accuracy for that mode (#req-qopt-break-even): ~0.93 for the
  whole list, ~0.89 (kind) / ~0.80 (area) for top-30 reorder. Below that it becomes a soft boost
  with weight scaled by p, or a ranker feature (#req-qopt-ltr-features).
- The gate also governs B1/B2: a rule-found cue becomes a constraint only if the gate agrees.
  That is what keeps "decode into a **struct**" pure.

Labels: a query is decomposable when the structure is stated in it, not when the gold happens to
have a kind. Training data, built and trained on Colab:
- positives by injecting structure into NL queries and intent-card texts: a real identifier, a
  real directory, "class `<Name>`", "tests for `<fn>`", "who calls `<fn>`";
- hard negatives: NL that uses kind words as English (the 15 bench cases above and generated
  ones);
- the dev query set's training split. Evaluation is leave-one-repo-out.

There are two inputs to compare:
- the dense query embedding, ~0 extra cost but possibly redundant with the ranking (as the
  top-k vote was);
- a text-only encoder over character n-grams / hashed word pieces.

Done when:
- the gate's AUROC and calibration (ECE, reliability plot) are reported on the bench and the
  dev set;
- each head's accuracy where it fires clears #req-qopt-break-even for the mode it drives;
- leave-one-repo-out ΔMRR on the bench is ≥ 0 and ΔR@10 on the dev set has a CI excluding 0;
- p95 latency on the laptop CPU is < 2 ms.

requirement.text:

- each head's accuracy where it fires clears #req-qopt-break-even for the mode it drives;

requirement.title: training and eval data come from the corpus, with its test split held out
requirement.text:
The encoder's corpus (`anvesa-corpus/work/`, Drive `MyDrive/anvesa-corpus/work/`):
- 187 indexed repos in 13 languages;
- 1.23M symbol cards, each with `kind`, `group`, `file`, `text` and `code`;
- `split.json`: 105 train, 26 val, 58 test repos.

**Sampling.** The optimizer's synthetic (query, decomposition, gold) triples are sampled per
language from **train** cards. The kinds the WQL part may target come from each card's `kind`.
For C#, the new `csharp.json` mapping gives class, method, interface, enum, struct and property.
Thresholds and calibration are fit on **val**.

**Held out.** No optimizer model, rule threshold or prompt is fit on test-split repos, for the
same leakage reason as the encoder. All 8 gen-lab bench repos are in the test split (checked
2026-10-27), so the bench stays a clean evaluation.

Done when:
- the sampler's output records each triple's repo and split;
- a check fails the build if a test-split repo appears in any training or calibration file.

requirement.title: per-language limits on what the optimizer emits
requirement.text:
A table, in code, of which constraint kinds the optimizer may emit per language, derived from the
mappings' real coverage. Initially:
- no `[@name]` on C/C++ functions;
- no property kind for C#;
- no constant/variable kind for Go var blocks until #req-go-var-blocks.

The oracle run (#req-qopt-oracle) lists the WQL that failed by language. That list is the
evidence for each row.

Outline coverage per language (`coverage.jsonl`, the last row per repo, mean of `covered`, read
2026-10-27):

| language | coverage |
|---|---|
| python | 0.89 |
| tsx | 0.88 |
| ruby | 0.88 |
| rust | 0.86 |
| csharp | 0.81 |
| typescript | 0.80 |
| java | 0.79 |
| vue | 0.68 |
| go | 0.65 |
| php | 0.58 |
| javascript | 0.51 |
| c | 0.13 |
| cpp | 0.13 |

Where coverage is low, a structural clause cannot reach most symbols. Below a coverage threshold
(start at 0.6, tune on val), the optimizer falls back to NL only: no kind or name clause, at most
a path scope. The gate's training labels follow the same rule, so it learns not to fire there.

**A default ruleset for languages trained on the fly.** A language whose mapping comes from

applies. Done when a test trains a mapping on samples of a language with no row and checks that
the optimizer emits only what that ruleset allows.

requirement.title: the break-even curve is part of every predictor's report
requirement.text:
`qopt.py` reports, for kind, directory and identifier constraints, the noisy-oracle curve (MRR
and R@10 vs error rate *p*), per combination mode. Each predictor's report then gives three
numbers: how often it fires, how accurate it is where it fires, and where that accuracy lands on
the curve.

A predictor proceeds only if its measured accuracy is above break-even for the mode it would use.

requirement.title: a query set phrased the way developers type
training and eval data come from the corpus, with its test split held out
requirement.text:
The encoder's corpus (`anvesa-corpus/work/`, Drive `MyDrive/anvesa-corpus/work/`):
- 187 indexed repos in 13 languages;
- 1.23M symbol cards, each with `kind`, `group`, `file`, `text` and `code`;
- `split.json`: 105 train, 26 val, 58 test repos.

**Sampling.** The optimizer's synthetic (query, decomposition, gold) triples are sampled per
language from **train** cards. The kinds the WQL part may target come from each card's `kind`.
For C#, the new `csharp.json` mapping gives class, method, interface, enum, struct and property.
Thresholds and calibration are fit on **val**.

**Held out.** No optimizer model, rule threshold or prompt is fit on test-split repos, for the
same leakage reason as the encoder. All 8 gen-lab bench repos are in the test split (checked
2026-10-27), so the bench stays a clean evaluation.

Done when:
- the sampler's output records each triple's repo and split;
- a check fails the build if a test-split repo appears in any training or calibration file.

annotation.author: nimis
annotation.body: Measured 2026-10-29 (gen-lab e801013, qopt.py oracle; output in results/qopt-oracle-2026-10-29.txt). 60 blind WQLs, all parse, none empty, median match set 4 symbols. R@10 on the sample: s1 0.600 -> 0.983 fused / 0.967 hard / 0.900 soft / 0.883 top30; s2 (XGBoost stack) 0.700 -> 1.000 fused / 0.983 hard. dR@10 CI s1 fused [+0.267,+0.500]. H1 holds far above +0.02. One WQL excluded its gold (viper-default-type, go): hard/prefilter drop it 1 -> 395, fused/top30 keep it at 3. Caveat: the WQLs are near-answers (tiny match sets), so this is an upper bound; predictability (H2) is the real question.

annotation.author: nimis
annotation.body: Measured 2026-10-29 (gen-lab d06a080, qopt.py breakeven; results/qopt-breakeven-2026-10-29.txt). Accuracy needed to break even on MRR (s1/s2): kind hard/fused 92-93%, top30 87-88%, soft 85-86%; dir hard/fused 91-93%, top30 80-82%, soft 73-74%; name soft/top30 never falls below the first stage up to 70% wrong, name hard 67-71%. Kind-word rule: fires 9%, 29% accurate, clears no mode. Soft uses a fixed +20 places, not tuned.
